title: A Grandson's Podcast About His Grandma's Dementia Wins Big Prize—and Opens Hearts
summary: What do you do when someone you love is changing and you don't know how to talk about it? Colby McCaskill, a 21-year-old college student, made a podcast. And it just won a huge prize! Colby's grandmother, Kathy, has dementia. That's a brain condition that makes it hard to remember things, even names or how to do simple tasks. Colby was scared and sad watching his Grammy change. So he created an audio letter to his grandpa, Dick. In the podcast, called "Dear Papa," Colby shares his worries. "It's hard to admit because it feels like there's no solution, but I really wish you and Grammy weren't growing so old," he says. He also records real moments with his grandparents, like them coloring together. Coloring helps Kathy feel calm and keeps her brain active. In one part, Kathy tries to say her age. "I think right now, I am like... 47 years old," she says with a laugh. Colby doesn't hide the hard stuff. He uses the word "dementia" clearly. His grandpa says hearing it was "like a cold cup of water thrown in your face"—but it helped him face the truth. Dick has listened to the podcast many times, and it always brings tears. But they're not just sad tears. They're tears of love, because Colby found a way to say what the whole family was feeling. The judges at NPR loved how honest and close the podcast felt. Out of hundreds of entries, Colby's story stood out. He says being with his grandparents is "like a warm hug," and his podcast is a gift that hugs them back—even when words are hard to find.
why_it_matters: When someone in your family gets ill in a way that changes who they are, finding a way to talk about it—like Colby did—can help everyone feel less alone and turn tough moments into loving memories.

background_read: Dementia is the name for a group of brain illnesses, like Alzheimer’s disease, that slowly make it harder to remember, think clearly, and look after yourself.
NPR stands for National Public Radio in the United States. It runs a College Podcast Challenge every year where university students send in their own audio stories.
Many families dealing with dementia find it tough to talk about, but sharing real moments—even sad ones—can help everyone feel closer and more understood.
Article_Structure: WHO: Colby McCaskill (college student), his grandmother Kathy (Grammy), his grandfather Dick (Papa)
WHAT: Colby made a podcast audio letter to his grandpa about Grammy’s dementia and won NPR’s podcast contest
WHERE: The podcast was recorded at home with his grandparents and entered in a US-wide competition
WHY: Colby wanted to express his fears and love honestly, and the podcast helped his family face the truth about dementia together

perspectives.description: Felt scared and sad but believed making the podcast was a way to be truthful and give his grandparents a gift of love that lasts.
Found the podcast painful like a ‘cold cup of water’ at first, but now listens to it many times and feels the tears are mainly love.
Saw the podcast as unusually honest and close, standing out from hundreds of entries because it didn't hide the hard parts.
Hearing the story might help others in similar families feel it’s okay to talk about dementia openly and find comfort in shared moments.
